claim: Lon is a highly conserved protease with important regulatory and protein quality control functions in cells from the three domains of life.
source: The highly conserved protease Lon has important regulatory and protein quality control functions in cells from the three domains of life.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about Lon protease.

claim: Only a few specific protein substrates of Lon are known in most organisms despite many years of research.
source: Despite many years of research on Lon, only a few specific protein substrates are known in most organisms.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field as described in the abstract.

claim: Lon recognizes StaR and FliK at their C-termini.
source: We show that Lon recognizes these proteins at their C-termini, and that Lon-dependent degradation ensures their temporally restricted accumulation in the cell cycle phase when their function is needed.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: Lon-dependent degradation ensures temporally restricted accumulation of StaR and FliK in the cell cycle phase when their function is needed.
source: We show that Lon recognizes these proteins at their C-termini, and that Lon-dependent degradation ensures their temporally restricted accumulation in the cell cycle phase when their function is needed.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell cycle synchronization experiments shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Disruption of temporal regulation of StaR and FliK levels in a Δlon mutant contributes to defects in stalk biogenesis and motility.
source: Disruption of this precise temporal regulation of StaR and FliK levels in a Δlon mutant contributes to defects in stalk biogenesis and motility, respectively, revealing a critical role of Lon in coordinating developmental processes with cell cycle progression.
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic analysis shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Lon has a critical role in coordinating developmental processes with cell cycle progression.
source: Disruption of this precise temporal regulation of StaR and FliK levels in a Δlon mutant contributes to defects in stalk biogenesis and motility, respectively, revealing a critical role of Lon in coordinating developmental processes with cell cycle progression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: This study includes the first characterization of FliK in C. crescentus.
source: Furthermore, this study includes the first characterization of FliK in C. crescentus and uncovers a dual role of the C-terminal amino acids of FliK in protein function and degradation.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution of the study.

claim: The C-terminal amino acids of FliK have a dual role in protein function and degradation.
source: Furthermore, this study includes the first characterization of FliK in C. crescentus and uncovers a dual role of the C-terminal amino acids of FliK in protein function and degradation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Lon was the first ATP-dependent protease to be identified.
source: The protease Lon was the first ATP-dependent protease to be identified and is widely conserved across the three domains of life (Gur, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Gur, 2013.

claim: Lon is widely conserved across the three domains of life.
source: The protease Lon was the first ATP-dependent protease to be identified and is widely conserved across the three domains of life (Gur, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Gur, 2013.

claim: Lon forms a hexameric protease complex.
source: Lon forms a hexameric protease complex, of which each monomer contains three functional domains: an N-terminal domain, an ATP-dependent unfoldase domain, and a peptidase domain forming the proteolytic chamber (Gur, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Gur, 2013.

claim: Each Lon monomer contains three functional domains: an N-terminal domain, an ATP-dependent unfoldase domain, and a peptidase domain forming the proteolytic chamber.
source: Lon forms a hexameric protease complex, of which each monomer contains three functional domains: an N-terminal domain, an ATP-dependent unfoldase domain, and a peptidase domain forming the proteolytic chamber (Gur, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Gur, 2013.

claim: Lon is a heat shock protein.
source: As a heat shock protein (Phillips et al., 1984), Lon is upregulated in response to protein unfolding stress, such as thermal stress, and contributes to the degradation of unfolded and misfolded proteins that accumulate under these conditions (Gur, 2013; Gur and Sauer, 2008; Tomoyasu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from Phillips et al., 1984.

claim: Lon is upregulated in response to protein unfolding stress, such as thermal stress.
source: As a heat shock protein (Phillips et al., 1984), Lon is upregulated in response to protein unfolding stress, such as thermal stress, and contributes to the degradation of unfolded and misfolded proteins that accumulate under these conditions (Gur, 2013; Gur and Sauer, 2008; Tomoyasu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources including Gur, 2013; Gur and Sauer, 2008; Tomoyasu et al., 2001.

claim: Lon contributes to the degradation of unfolded and misfolded proteins that accumulate under stress conditions.
source: As a heat shock protein (Phillips et al., 1984), Lon is upregulated in response to protein unfolding stress, such as thermal stress, and contributes to the degradation of unfolded and misfolded proteins that accumulate under these conditions (Gur, 2013; Gur and Sauer, 2008; Tomoyasu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from Gur, 2013; Gur and Sauer, 2008; Tomoyasu et al., 2001.

claim: Lon exerts important regulatory functions through degradation of specific sets of native substrate proteins involved in stress responses, metabolism, pathogenicity, and cell cycle progression.
source: In addition to its role in protein quality control, Lon exerts important regulatory functions that can be traced to the degradation of specific sets of native substrate proteins involved in stress responses, metabolism, pathogenicity, and cell cycle progression (Tsilibaris et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Tsilibaris et al., 2006.

claim: In E. coli, Lon specifically degrades several stress-induced regulators.
source: In Escherichia coli, Lon specifically degrades several stress-induced regulators (Griffith et al., 2004; Langklotz and Narberhaus, 2011; Mizusawa and Gottesman, 1983), metabolic enzymes (Arends et al., 2018) as well as antitoxins of toxin-antitoxin systems (Muthuramalingam et al., 2016), and in several pathogenic bacteria, Lon was shown to degrade regulators of pathogenicity (Joshi et al., 2020; Puri and Karzai, 2017), thus playing important roles in the regulation of virulence pathways.
evidence: This is cited from Griffith et al., 2004; Langklotz and Narberhaus, 2011; Mizusawa and Gottesman, 1983.

claim: In E. coli, Lon degrades metabolic enzymes.
source: In Escherichia coli, Lon specifically degrades several stress-induced regulators (Griffith et al., 2004; Langklotz and Narberhaus, 2011; Mizusawa and Gottesman, 1983), metabolic enzymes (Arends et al., 2018) as well as antitoxins of toxin-antitoxin systems (Muthuramalingam et al., 2016), and in several pathogenic bacteria, Lon was shown to degrade regulators of pathogenicity (Joshi et al., 2020; Puri and Karzai, 2017), thus playing important roles in the regulation of virulence pathways.
evidence: This is cited from Arends et al., 2018.

claim: In E. coli, Lon degrades antitoxins of toxin-antitoxin systems.
source: In Escherichia coli, Lon specifically degrades several stress-induced regulators (Griffith et al., 2004; Langklotz and Narberhaus, 2011; Mizusawa and Gottesman, 1983), metabolic enzymes (Arends et al., 2018) as well as antitoxins of toxin-antitoxin systems (Muthuramalingam et al., 2016), and in several pathogenic bacteria, Lon was shown to degrade regulators of pathogenicity (Joshi et al., 2020; Puri and Karzai, 2017), thus playing important roles in the regulation of virulence pathways.
evidence: This is cited from Muthuramalingam et al., 2016.

claim: In several pathogenic bacteria, Lon degrades regulators of pathogenicity, playing important roles in the regulation of virulence pathways.
source: In Escherichia coli, Lon specifically degrades several stress-induced regulators (Griffith et al., 2004; Langklotz and Narberhaus, 2011; Mizusawa and Gottesman, 1983), metabolic enzymes (Arends et al., 2018) as well as antitoxins of toxin-antitoxin systems (Muthuramalingam et al., 2016), and in several pathogenic bacteria, Lon was shown to degrade regulators of pathogenicity (Joshi et al., 2020; Puri and Karzai, 2017), thus playing important roles in the regulation of virulence pathways.
evidence: This is cited from Joshi et al., 2020; Puri and Karzai, 2017.

claim: In C. crescentus, Lon impacts cell cycle progression by degrading essential cell cycle regulators.
source: In the alpha-proteobacterium Caulobacter crescentus, the number of identified Lon substrates to date is small, however, Lon is known to impact cell cycle progression by degrading essential cell cycle regulators.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Lon in C. crescentus.

claim: The C. crescentus cell cycle is characterized by an asymmetric cell division event and morphologically distinct cell cycle phases.
source: The C. crescentus cell cycle is characterized by an asymmetric cell division event and morphologically distinct cell cycle phases (Curtis and Brun, 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Curtis and Brun, 2010.

claim: Each C. crescentus division yields a flagellated and piliated swarmer cell and a sessile stalked cell.
source: Each division yields a flagellated and piliated swarmer cell and a sessile stalked cell.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about C. crescentus cell division.

claim: The daughter stalked cell initiates DNA replication immediately after cell division.
source: While the daughter stalked cell initiates DNA replication immediately after cell division, the daughter swarmer cell must differentiate into a stalked cell before entering S-phase.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about C. crescentus cell cycle.

claim: The daughter swarmer cell must differentiate into a stalked cell before entering S-phase.
source: While the daughter stalked cell initiates DNA replication immediately after cell division, the daughter swarmer cell must differentiate into a stalked cell before entering S-phase.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about C. crescentus cell cycle.

claim: Around one-third of all genes in C. crescentus show cell cycle-dependent fluctuations in their expression levels.
source: Previous work established that around one-third of all genes in C. crescentus show cell cycle-dependent fluctuations in their expression levels (Fang et al., 2013; Laub et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited from Fang et al., 2013; Laub et al., 2000.

claim: Many proteins with important developmental functions peak in abundance in the cell cycle phase in which their function is most needed.
source: Many of the corresponding proteins have important developmental functions and peak in abundance in the cell cycle phase in which their function is most needed (Laub et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited from Laub et al., 2000.

claim: Active proteolysis must occur to rapidly adjust protein concentrations to enforce transcriptional changes.
source: In addition to transcriptional regulatory mechanisms, active proteolysis must occur to rapidly adjust protein concentrations to enforce these transcriptional changes (Grünenfelder et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from Grünenfelder et al., 2001.

claim: The ClpP protease with its unfoldases ClpA and ClpX has key roles in C. crescentus development by mediating temporally and spatially controlled degradation of several important cell cycle regulators.
source: Previous work established that the ClpP protease with its unfoldases ClpA and ClpX has key roles in C. crescentus development by mediating the temporally and spatially controlled degradation of several important cell cycle regulators (Joshi and Chien, 2016; Schroeder and Jonas, 2021).
evidence: This is cited from Joshi and Chien, 2016; Schroeder and Jonas, 2021.

claim: Lon plays an important role in C. crescentus cell cycle regulation.
source: In addition to ClpXP, Lon plays an important role in C. crescentus cell cycle regulation (Joshi and Chien, 2016; Schroeder and Jonas, 2021).
evidence: This is cited from Joshi and Chien, 2016; Schroeder and Jonas, 2021.

claim: Lon degrades the swarmer cell-specific transcription factor SciP.
source: It degrades the swarmer cell-specific transcription factor SciP (Gora et al., 2013), the methyltransferase and transcriptional regulator CcrM (Wright et al., 1996), and the conserved replication initiator DnaA (Jonas et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Gora et al., 2013.

claim: Lon degrades the methyltransferase and transcriptional regulator CcrM.
source: It degrades the swarmer cell-specific transcription factor SciP (Gora et al., 2013), the methyltransferase and transcriptional regulator CcrM (Wright et al., 1996), and the conserved replication initiator DnaA (Jonas et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Wright et al., 1996.

claim: Lon degrades the conserved replication initiator DnaA.
source: It degrades the swarmer cell-specific transcription factor SciP (Gora et al., 2013), the methyltransferase and transcriptional regulator CcrM (Wright et al., 1996), and the conserved replication initiator DnaA (Jonas et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Jonas et al., 2013.

claim: Lon-dependent degradation of SciP and CcrM contributes to their cell cycle-dependent regulation.
source: Lon-dependent degradation of SciP and CcrM contributes to their cell cycle-dependent regulation (Gora et al., 2013; Wright et al., 1996), while DnaA degradation by Lon ensures rapid clearance of the protein at the onset of nutritional and proteotoxic stress, preventing cell cycle progression under these conditions (Felletti et al., 2019; Jonas et al., 2013; Leslie et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Gora et al., 2013; Wright et al., 1996.

claim: DnaA degradation by Lon ensures rapid clearance of the protein at the onset of nutritional and proteotoxic stress, preventing cell cycle progression under these conditions.
source: Lon-dependent degradation of SciP and CcrM contributes to their cell cycle-dependent regulation (Gora et al., 2013; Wright et al., 1996), while DnaA degradation by Lon ensures rapid clearance of the protein at the onset of nutritional and proteotoxic stress, preventing cell cycle progression under these conditions (Felletti et al., 2019; Jonas et al., 2013; Leslie et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Felletti et al., 2019; Jonas et al., 2013; Leslie et al., 2015.

claim: C. crescentus cells lacking Lon are viable.
source: Although C. crescentus cells lacking Lon are viable, they grow more slowly and show aberrant chromosome content and division defects (Leslie et al., 2015; Wright et al., 1996), which can in part be attributed to the stabilization of DnaA, SciP, and CcrM.
evidence: This is cited from Leslie et al., 2015; Wright et al., 1996.

claim: C. crescentus cells lacking Lon grow more slowly and show aberrant chromosome content and division defects.
source: Although C. crescentus cells lacking Lon are viable, they grow more slowly and show aberrant chromosome content and division defects (Leslie et al., 2015; Wright et al., 1996), which can in part be attributed to the stabilization of DnaA, SciP, and CcrM.
evidence: This is cited from Leslie et al., 2015; Wright et al., 1996.

claim: The growth and division defects in Δlon cells can in part be attributed to the stabilization of DnaA, SciP, and CcrM.
source: Although C. crescentus cells lacking Lon are viable, they grow more slowly and show aberrant chromosome content and division defects (Leslie et al., 2015; Wright et al., 1996), which can in part be attributed to the stabilization of DnaA, SciP, and CcrM.
evidence: This is cited from Leslie et al., 2015; Wright et al., 1996.

claim: Δlon cells exhibit elongated stalks and motility defects.
source: Interestingly, Δlon cells exhibit also characteristic developmental defects, that is, elongated stalks and motility defects (Wright et al., 1996; Yang et al., 2018), suggesting that Lon degrades additional substrates involved in cell differentiation.
evidence: This is cited from Wright et al., 1996; Yang et al., 2018.

claim: The developmental defects in Δlon cells suggest that Lon degrades additional substrates involved in cell differentiation.
source: Interestingly, Δlon cells exhibit also characteristic developmental defects, that is, elongated stalks and motility defects (Wright et al., 1996; Yang et al., 2018), suggesting that Lon degrades additional substrates involved in cell differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed phenotypes cited from Wright et al., 1996; Yang et al., 2018.

claim: DnaA, CcrM, and SciP are more stable in the Δlon strain compared to the WT.
source: Absence of Lon, either in a Δlon strain or following Lon depletion, results in increased stability and abundance of these proteins (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: DnaA, CcrM, and SciP show increased steady-state levels in Δlon and Lon-depleted cells.
source: Absence of Lon, either in a Δlon strain or following Lon depletion, results in increased stability and abundance of these proteins (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: lon overexpression leads to lower protein abundance of DnaA, CcrM, and SciP.
source: Conversely, lon overexpression leads to lower protein abundance of DnaA, CcrM, and SciP (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 26 proteins fulfilled all four criteria for being putative Lon substrates, one of them being DnaA.
source: We identified 26 proteins that fulfilled all four criteria, one of them being DnaA.
evidence: This is based on the proteomics analysis described in the Results section.

claim: 120 proteins fulfilled three criteria for being putative Lon substrates.
source: 120 proteins fulfilled three criteria, and because CcrM and SciP were in this group of proteins (Figure 1D), we considered proteins satisfying either three or four criteria as putative Lon substrates.
evidence: This is based on the proteomics analysis described in the Results section and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CcrM and SciP were in the group of proteins that fulfilled three criteria.
source: 120 proteins fulfilled three criteria, and because CcrM and SciP were in this group of proteins (Figure 1D), we considered proteins satisfying either three or four criteria as putative Lon substrates.
evidence: This is based on the proteomics analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 146 proteins satisfied either three or four criteria and were considered putative Lon substrates.
source: The 146 proteins that fell into this group contained proteins from all major functional categories (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on the proteomics analysis shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: The group of putative Lon substrates contained a lower proportion of metabolic proteins and proteins involved in core genetic information processing compared to all detected proteins.
source: In comparison to all detected proteins, the group of putative Lon substrates contained a lower proportion of metabolic proteins and proteins involved in core genetic information processing, whereas proteins involved in cell cycle and cell differentiation processes, signal transduction and stress responses as well as unclassified proteins showed a higher relative abundance (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on functional categorization of the proteomics data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Proteins involved in cell cycle and cell differentiation processes, signal transduction and stress responses as well as unclassified proteins showed a higher relative abundance in the group of putative Lon substrates compared to all detected proteins.
source: In comparison to all detected proteins, the group of putative Lon substrates contained a lower proportion of metabolic proteins and proteins involved in core genetic information processing, whereas proteins involved in cell cycle and cell differentiation processes, signal transduction and stress responses as well as unclassified proteins showed a higher relative abundance (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on functional categorization of the proteomics data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: FixT and HipB2 were not detected in the proteomics experiment.
source: Notably, we did not detect FixT and HipB2 in our proteomics experiment, two other recently reported Lon substrates in C. crescentus (Stein et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the proteomics experiment, with citations to studies that identified these as Lon substrates.

claim: FixT and HipB2 are recently reported Lon substrates in C. crescentus.
source: Notably, we did not detect FixT and HipB2 in our proteomics experiment, two other recently reported Lon substrates in C. crescentus (Stein et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from Stein et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2021.

claim: StaR was one of the proteins that satisfied the four criteria in the proteomics experiment most clearly.
source: One of the proteins that satisfied the four criteria in our proteomics experiment most clearly was the transcriptional regulator StaR, a protein previously reported to be involved in the regulation of stalk biogenesis and holdfast production (Figure 1D and F; Biondi et al., 2006; Fiebig et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on the proteomics data shown in Figure 1D and F.

claim: StaR is a transcriptional regulator previously reported to be involved in the regulation of stalk biogenesis and holdfast production.
source: One of the proteins that satisfied the four criteria in our proteomics experiment most clearly was the transcriptional regulator StaR, a protein previously reported to be involved in the regulation of stalk biogenesis and holdfast production (Figure 1D and F; Biondi et al., 2006; Fiebig et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Biondi et al., 2006; Fiebig et al., 2014.

claim: StaR was more stable in the Δlon strain compared to the WT.
source: Like the three known substrates DnaA, CcrM, and SciP, StaR was more stable in the Δlon strain compared to the WT and showed increased steady-state levels in Δlon and Lon-depleted cells, but reduced protein levels in cells overexpressing lon (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on proteomics data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: StaR showed increased steady-state levels in Δlon and Lon-depleted cells.
source: Like the three known substrates DnaA, CcrM, and SciP, StaR was more stable in the Δlon strain compared to the WT and showed increased steady-state levels in Δlon and Lon-depleted cells, but reduced protein levels in cells overexpressing lon (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on proteomics data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: StaR showed reduced protein levels in cells overexpressing lon.
source: Like the three known substrates DnaA, CcrM, and SciP, StaR was more stable in the Δlon strain compared to the WT and showed increased steady-state levels in Δlon and Lon-depleted cells, but reduced protein levels in cells overexpressing lon (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on proteomics data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the WT, the levels of StaR were below the limit of detection.
source: In the WT, the levels of StaR were below the limit of detection, however, we observed a strong and stable band corresponding to StaR in the Δlon strain (Figure 2B), indicating that StaR is upregulated in Δlon cells, a result that is consistent with the proteomics data (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A strong and stable band corresponding to StaR was observed in the Δlon strain.
source: In the WT, the levels of StaR were below the limit of detection, however, we observed a strong and stable band corresponding to StaR in the Δlon strain (Figure 2B), indicating that StaR is upregulated in Δlon cells, a result that is consistent with the proteomics data (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: StaR is upregulated in Δlon cells.
source: In the WT, the levels of StaR were below the limit of detection, however, we observed a strong and stable band corresponding to StaR in the Δlon strain (Figure 2B), indicating that StaR is upregulated in Δlon cells, a result that is consistent with the proteomics data (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is inferred from Western blot data shown in Figure 2B and is consistent with proteomics data in Figure 2A.

claim: StaR was degraded with a half-life of approximately 12 min when Lon was present.
source: In this strain, StaR was degraded with a half-life of approximately 12 min, when Lon was present (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on in vivo degradation assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Absence of Lon resulted in complete stabilization of StaR and increased steady-state levels.
source: Absence of Lon resulted again in complete stabilization of StaR and increased steady-state levels, which is in line with our proteomics data, and confirms that StaR degradation depends on Lon.
evidence: This is based on in vivo degradation assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: StaR degradation depends on Lon.
source: Absence of Lon resulted again in complete stabilization of StaR and increased steady-state levels, which is in line with our proteomics data, and confirms that StaR degradation depends on Lon.
evidence: This is confirmed by in vivo degradation assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Lon readily degrades StaR in an ATP-dependent manner in vitro.
source: This assay showed that Lon readily degrades StaR in an ATP-dependent manner (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on in vitro degradation assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: StaR is a Lon substrate and no additional factors are required for recognizing and degrading StaR, at least in vitro.
source: Hence, StaR is a Lon substrate and no additional factors are required for recognizing and degrading StaR, at least in vitro.
evidence: This is concluded from the in vitro degradation assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Addition of the 3xFLAG tag to the C-terminus of StaR completely abolished degradation.
source: Addition of the 3xFLAG tag to the C-terminus of StaR (StaR-F) completely abolished degradation (Figure 2E), indicating that a freely accessible C-terminus of StaR is required for degradation by Lon.
evidence: This is based on in vivo degradation assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A freely accessible C-terminus of StaR is required for degradation by Lon.
source: Addition of the 3xFLAG tag to the C-terminus of StaR (StaR-F) completely abolished degradation (Figure 2E), indicating that a freely accessible C-terminus of StaR is required for degradation by Lon.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that C-terminal tagging abolished degradation, as shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Addition of the 3xFLAG tag to the N-terminus of StaR still enabled notable degradation within 60 min after shutting down protein synthesis.
source: Addition of the tag to the N-terminus of StaR (F-StaR) still enabled notable degradation within 60 min after shutting down protein synthesis (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on in vivo degradation assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Degradation of N-terminally tagged StaR was also observed in the Δlon strain, suggesting that another protease degrades this StaR variant.
source: However, degradation of this N-terminally tagged StaR was also observed in the Δlon strain, suggesting that another protease degrades this StaR variant, probably because of changes in StaR folding that result from the addition of the tag.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that N-terminally tagged StaR is degraded even in Δlon cells, as shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Native N-termini and C-termini of StaR are required for Lon-dependent degradation.
source: These data show that native N-termini and C-termini of the protein are required for Lon-dependent degradation.
evidence: This is concluded from the tagging experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: StaR function is expected to be particularly needed at the beginning of the cell cycle, when the swarmer cell differentiates into a stalked cell.
source: As a transcriptional regulator of stalk biogenesis and holdfast production, StaR function is expected to be particularly needed at the beginning of the cell cycle, when the swarmer cell differentiates into a stalked cell (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is inferred from the known function of StaR and the cell cycle diagram shown in Figure 3A.

claim: staR mRNA levels fluctuate during the cell cycle, peaking in the swarmer and early stalked cell before declining during S-phase and remaining low until cell division.
source: Indeed, previously published RNA sequencing data show that staR mRNA levels fluctuate during the cell cycle, peaking in the swarmer and early stalked cell before declining during S-phase and remaining low until cell division (Figure 3B; Lasker et al., 2016; Schrader et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Lasker et al., 2016; Schrader et al., 2016 and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: StaR is translated predominantly in the swarmer and early stalked cells, but only at low levels during the remaining cell cycle.
source: Furthermore, existing ribosome profiling data show that StaR is translated predominantly in the swarmer and early stalked cells, but only at low levels during the remaining cell cycle (Lasker et al., 2016; Schrader et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Lasker et al., 2016; Schrader et al., 2016.

claim: StaR protein levels follow the expression pattern in WT cultures, being detectable within 30 min after synchronization before being strongly downregulated.
source: Quantification of StaR protein levels by Western blot analysis in synchronized cultures showed that protein levels follow this expression pattern in WT cultures (Figure 3C). StaR was detectable within 30 min after synchronization before it was strongly downregulated and remained below the limit of detection for the rest of the cell cycle.
evidence: This is based on Western blot data from synchronized cultures shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The cell cycle-dependent changes in StaR protein abundance were absent in the Δlon strain, in which StaR levels remained high until 75 min after synchronization.
source: Strikingly, the cell cycle-dependent changes in protein abundance were absent in the Δlon strain, in which StaR levels remained high until 75 min after synchronization (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on Western blot data from synchronized cultures shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Lon-dependent degradation of StaR is required for establishing oscillations of StaR levels during the cell cycle.
source: Thus, Lon-dependent degradation of StaR is required for establishing oscillations of StaR levels during the cell cycle.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that StaR levels do not oscillate in Δlon cells, as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The stalks of Δlon cells are significantly elongated compared to the WT.
source: Consistent with a previous study (Wright et al., 1996), we observed that the stalks of Δlon cells are significantly elongated compared to the WT (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is based on microscopy and stalk length measurements shown in Figure 3D-E, and is consistent with Wright et al., 1996.

claim: StaR overexpression leads to an increase of stalk length.
source: Because StaR overexpression was shown to lead to an increase of stalk length (Biondi et al., 2006), we reasoned that the abnormal stalk length of Δlon cells might be caused by the higher abundance of StaR in these cells.
evidence: This is cited from Biondi et al., 2006.

claim: The abnormal stalk length of Δlon cells might be caused by the higher abundance of StaR in these cells.
source: Because StaR overexpression was shown to lead to an increase of stalk length (Biondi et al., 2006), we reasoned that the abnormal stalk length of Δlon cells might be caused by the higher abundance of StaR in these cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known effect of StaR overexpression cited from Biondi et al., 2006.

claim: The ΔstaR Δlon mutant phenocopied the ΔstaR single mutant, in which stalks are shortened compared to Δlon cells.
source: The ΔstaR Δlon mutant phenocopied the ΔstaR single mutant, in which stalks are shortened compared to Δlon cells, demonstrating that Lon affects stalk length through StaR (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is based on stalk length measurements shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: Lon affects stalk length through StaR.
source: The ΔstaR Δlon mutant phenocopied the ΔstaR single mutant, in which stalks are shortened compared to Δlon cells, demonstrating that Lon affects stalk length through StaR (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is concluded from the genetic epistasis experiment shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: All four strains (WT, ΔstaR, Δlon, ΔstaR Δlon) were able to strongly elongate their stalks under phosphate starvation.
source: However, all four strains were able to strongly elongate their stalks under phosphate starvation, suggesting that StaR and Lon are not required for starvation-dependent stalk elongation.
evidence: This is based on stalk length measurements under phosphate starvation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: StaR and Lon are not required for starvation-dependent stalk elongation.
source: However, all four strains were able to strongly elongate their stalks under phosphate starvation, suggesting that StaR and Lon are not required for starvation-dependent stalk elongation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that all strains elongate stalks under starvation, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lon-mediated degradation of StaR is required for proper stalk biogenesis during the cell cycle.
source: Taken together, our data demonstrate that Lon-mediated degradation of StaR is required for proper stalk biogenesis during the cell cycle.
evidence: This is concluded from the stalk length phenotype data shown in Figures 3D-E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: CCNA_00944 and MotD (CCNA_00945) are encoded by partly overlapping open reading frames.
source: Particularly promising hits in this group of proteins were CCNA_00944 and MotD (CCNA_00945) that are encoded by partly overlapping open reading frames and showed similar changes in protein abundance and stability in the Lon deficient and Lon overproducing strains in our proteomics experiments (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is based on genome annotation and proteomics data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: CCNA_00944 and MotD showed similar changes in protein abundance and stability in the Lon deficient and Lon overproducing strains.
source: Particularly promising hits in this group of proteins were CCNA_00944 and MotD (CCNA_00945) that are encoded by partly overlapping open reading frames and showed similar changes in protein abundance and stability in the Lon deficient and Lon overproducing strains in our proteomics experiments (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is based on proteomics data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: CCNA_00944 is annotated as a flagella hook length determination protein.
source: While CCNA_00944 is annotated as a flagella hook length determination protein, MotD is annotated as a chemotaxis protein.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation.

claim: MotD is annotated as a chemotaxis protein.
source: While CCNA_00944 is annotated as a flagella hook length determination protein, MotD is annotated as a chemotaxis protein.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation.

claim: MotD contains a conserved Flg hook domain that is commonly present in the C-terminal portion of FliK proteins that control flagella hook length in many bacteria.
source: According to a signature-based annotation of MotD in UniProtKB (entry A0A0H3C6R3), MotD contains a conserved Flg hook domain that is commonly present in the C-terminal portion of FliK proteins that control flagella hook length in many bacteria (Waters et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on UniProtKB annotation and cited from Waters et al., 2007.

claim: An additional guanosine in the CCNA_00944 gene sequence generates a frameshift that merges the CCNA_00944 gene with the downstream located motD gene, forming one single open reading frame.
source: This insertion, which is also present in the sequence reads of previously published RNA-sequencing data (Schrader et al., 2014), generates a frameshift that merges the CCNA_00944 gene with the downstream located motD gene, thus forming one single open reading frame, of which the 3′ portion corresponds to motD (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on sequencing data and RNA-seq data cited from Schrader et al., 2014, and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CCNA_00944 and motD are incorrectly annotated in the reference genome of NA1000 and instead form one continuous open reading frame.
source: These observations indicate that CCNA_00944 and motD are incorrectly annotated in the reference genome of NA1000 and instead form one continuous open reading frame.
evidence: This is concluded from sequencing and RNA-seq data.

claim: Western blot analysis with antiserum raised against the protein portion corresponding to MotD detected one single protein band that runs at high molecular weight.
source: Consistently, when we performed Western blot analysis with antiserum raised against the protein portion corresponding to MotD, we detected one single protein band that runs at high molecular weight (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), confirming that CCNA_00944 and motD form together one single open reading frame.
evidence: This is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: CCNA_00944 and motD form together one single open reading frame.
source: Consistently, when we performed Western blot analysis with antiserum raised against the protein portion corresponding to MotD, we detected one single protein band that runs at high molecular weight (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), confirming that CCNA_00944 and motD form together one single open reading frame.
evidence: This is confirmed by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The merged gene was named fliK because the C-terminal portion encodes a Flg hook domain characteristic of FliK proteins in other bacteria.
source: Because the C-terminal portion of this new gene encodes a Flg hook domain that is a characteristic of FliK proteins in other bacteria and because no other gene has so far been annotated as fliK in C. crescentus, we named the new gene fliK (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on domain analysis and comparison to other bacteria.

claim: No other gene has been annotated as fliK in C. crescentus.
source: Because the C-terminal portion of this new gene encodes a Flg hook domain that is a characteristic of FliK proteins in other bacteria and because no other gene has so far been annotated as fliK in C. crescentus, we named the new gene fliK (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the C. crescentus genome annotation.

claim: A recent study in Sinorhizobium meliloti suggested that the motD gene from alpha-proteobacteria should be renamed fliK.
source: This annotation of fliK is also in line with a recent study in Sinorhizobium meliloti, which suggested that the motD gene from alpha-proteobacteria should be renamed fliK (Eggenhofer et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Eggenhofer et al., 2006.

claim: FliK abundance and stability were notably increased in Δlon cells.
source: Consistent with our proteomics data, we found that FliK abundance and stability were notably increased in Δlon cells, consistent with FliK being a Lon substrate (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on in vivo degradation assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: FliK is a Lon substrate.
source: Consistent with our proteomics data, we found that FliK abundance and stability were notably increased in Δlon cells, consistent with FliK being a Lon substrate (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is concluded from the increased abundance and stability in Δlon cells shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 3xFLAG-FliK was efficiently degraded in WT cells but stable in cells lacking Lon.
source: Similar to the non-tagged FliK, 3xFLAG-FliK was efficiently degraded in WT cells but stable in cells lacking Lon (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on in vivo degradation assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The recognition of FliK by Lon occurs via the C-terminal domain of FliK.
source: This result led us to hypothesize that the recognition by Lon occurs via the C-terminal domain of FliK.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that N-terminal tagging does not prevent degradation.

claim: Degradation of FliK-C (the C-terminal portion of FliK) depended strongly on Lon.
source: Like the full-length protein, degradation of this truncated FliK protein (FliK-C), with a FLAG-tag at the N-terminus, depended strongly on Lon (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on in vivo degradation assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Lon degrades FliK-C in an ATP-dependent manner in vitro.
source: Furthermore, in vitro degradation assays showed that Lon degrades non-tagged FliK-C in an ATP-dependent manner (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on in vitro degradation assay data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The C-terminal portion of FliK containing the Flg hook domain is sufficient for Lon-dependent degradation.
source: Based on these results, we conclude that FliK is a Lon substrate, and that its C-terminal portion containing the Flg hook domain is sufficient for Lon-dependent degradation.
evidence: This is concluded from the degradation assays of FliK-C shown in Figures 4E-F.

claim: Deletion of the unordered regions in FliK-C did not influence degradation.
source: In vitro degradation assays showed that deletion of the unordered regions did not influence degradation, whereas removal of the 44 C-terminal amino acids completely stabilized the protein (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on in vitro degradation assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Removal of the 44 C-terminal amino acids of FliK-C completely stabilized the protein.
source: In vitro degradation assays showed that deletion of the unordered regions did not influence degradation, whereas removal of the 44 C-terminal amino acids completely stabilized the protein (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on in vitro degradation assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Deletion of the C-terminal five amino acids (LDIRI) of FliK-C abolished degradation.
source: This deletion abolished FliK-C degradation (Figure 4G), demonstrating that the interaction between Lon and FliK depends on these C-terminal amino acids.
evidence: This is based on in vivo degradation assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The interaction between Lon and FliK depends on the C-terminal five amino acids (LDIRI).
source: This deletion abolished FliK-C degradation (Figure 4G), demonstrating that the interaction between Lon and FliK depends on these C-terminal amino acids.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that deletion of these amino acids abolishes degradation, as shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The transcription of fliK is cell cycle regulated, with mRNA levels and ribosome occupancy peaking in late S-phase.
source: Like many other proteins involved in flagella biogenesis in C. crescentus, the transcription of the two annotated genes CCNA_00944 and motD that together form the fliK gene is cell cycle regulated (Lasker et al., 2016; Schrader et al., 2016), with mRNA levels and ribosome occupancy peaking in late S-phase when a new flagellum at the pole opposite the stalk is being assembled (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is cited from Lasker et al., 2016; Schrader et al., 2016 and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: FliK protein was not detectable in the beginning of the cell cycle in WT cells, but began to accumulate in late stalked cells before reaching a maximum in abundance in predivisional cells shortly before cell division.
source: Consistently, Western blot analysis with synchronized WT C. crescentus cultures showed that FliK protein was not detectable in the beginning of the cell cycle, but began to accumulate in late stalked cells before reaching a maximum in abundance in predivisional cells shortly before cell division (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on Western blot data from synchronized cultures shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The cell cycle-dependent pattern of FliK abundance was completely absent in the Δlon strain, in which FliK was already detectable in swarmer cells and remained at high levels throughout the cell cycle.
source: This cell cycle-dependent pattern of FliK abundance was completely absent in the Δlon strain, in which FliK was already detectable in swarmer cells and remained at high levels throughout the cell cycle (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on Western blot data from synchronized cultures shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Lon is necessary to ensure that FliK is eliminated in the cell cycle phase when its function is no longer needed.
source: This result shows that, as in the case of StaR, Lon is absolutely necessary to ensure that the protein is eliminated in the cell cycle phase when its function is no longer needed.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that FliK levels do not oscillate in Δlon cells, as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Δlon cells show reduced motility in soft agar compared to the WT.
source: Consistent with a previous study (Yang et al., 2018), we observed that Δlon cells show reduced motility in soft agar compared to the WT (Figure 5C), which might be caused by reduced flagella function in addition to growth and cell division defects.
evidence: This is based on motility assay data shown in Figure 5C and is consistent with Yang et al., 2018.

claim: The reduced motility in Δlon cells might be caused by reduced flagella function in addition to growth and cell division defects.
source: Consistent with a previous study (Yang et al., 2018), we observed that Δlon cells show reduced motility in soft agar compared to the WT (Figure 5C), which might be caused by reduced flagella function in addition to growth and cell division defects.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed motility defect.

claim: The levels of α-flagellins FljJ, FljK, and FljL and β-flagellins FljM and FljN are strongly downregulated in the Δlon mutant.
source: Additionally, our proteomics data revealed that the levels of α-flagellins FljJ, FljK, and FljL and β-flagellins FljM and FljN, which compose the structural components of flagella, are strongly downregulated in the Δlon mutant (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on proteomics data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The stabilization and higher levels of SciP in the Δlon mutant might explain the motility defect and reduced flagellin levels.
source: One explanation for the motility defect and the reduced flagellin levels in the Δlon mutant might be the stabilization and higher levels of SciP in this strain (Figure 1A; Gora et al., 2013), which is known to negatively affect flagellin gene expression through CtrA (Gora et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on known effects of SciP cited from Gora et al., 2010; Gora et al., 2013.

claim: SciP negatively affects flagellin gene expression through CtrA.
source: One explanation for the motility defect and the reduced flagellin levels in the Δlon mutant might be the stabilization and higher levels of SciP in this strain (Figure 1A; Gora et al., 2013), which is known to negatively affect flagellin gene expression through CtrA (Gora et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Gora et al., 2010.

claim: Overexpression of FliK led to a reproducible reduction in swim diameter to 85% compared to the vector control strain.
source: Overexpression of FliK led indeed to a reproducible reduction in swim diameter to 85% compared to the vector control strain (Figure 5E), indicating that elevated levels of FliK impair motility.
evidence: This is based on motility assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Elevated levels of FliK impair motility.
source: Overexpression of FliK led indeed to a reproducible reduction in swim diameter to 85% compared to the vector control strain (Figure 5E), indicating that elevated levels of FliK impair motility.
evidence: This is concluded from the motility assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The effect of FliK overexpression on motility was clearly exacerbated in the strain overexpressing FliK-C.
source: Interestingly, while this effect was clearly exacerbated in the strain overexpressing FliK-C (Figure 5E–F), it was absent in the strain overexpressing FliK-CΔ5, demonstrating that the C-terminus of FliK is critical for the FliK-dependent effect on motility.
evidence: This is based on motility assay data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: The effect of FliK overexpression on motility was absent in the strain overexpressing FliK-CΔ5.
source: Interestingly, while this effect was clearly exacerbated in the strain overexpressing FliK-C (Figure 5E–F), it was absent in the strain overexpressing FliK-CΔ5, demonstrating that the C-terminus of FliK is critical for the FliK-dependent effect on motility.
evidence: This is based on motility assay data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: The C-terminus of FliK is critical for the FliK-dependent effect on motility.
source: Interestingly, while this effect was clearly exacerbated in the strain overexpressing FliK-C (Figure 5E–F), it was absent in the strain overexpressing FliK-CΔ5, demonstrating that the C-terminus of FliK is critical for the FliK-dependent effect on motility.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparison of FliK-C and FliK-CΔ5 overexpression effects shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: The motility defects of the FliK and FliK-C overexpression strains correlated with a significant downregulation of flagellin levels to 55% and 30%, respectively.
source: When analyzing flagellin protein levels in the different overexpression strains, we found that the motility defects of the FliK and FliK-C overexpression strains correlated with a significant downregulation of flagellin levels to 55% and 30%, respectively (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Overexpression of FliK-CΔ5 affected flagellin levels only mildly.
source: Conversely, overexpression of the FliK-CΔ5 affected flagellin levels only mildly (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: An oversupply of FliK leads to reduced motility and flagellin levels.
source: Taken together, our data indicate that an oversupply of FliK, which can either be caused by overexpression or absence of Lon-dependent degradation, leads to reduced motility and flagellin levels.
evidence: This is concluded from the overexpression and Δlon phenotype data shown in Figure 5.

claim: FliK likely contributes to the motility defects of Δlon cells along with SciP and potentially other Lon substrates affecting flagella function.
source: This suggests that FliK likely contributes to the motility defects of Δlon cells along with SciP and potentially other Lon substrates affecting flagella function that are stabilized and upregulated in the absence of Lon.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined effects of FliK and SciP on motility and flagellin levels.

claim: The C-terminal portion of FliK is critical for its effects on motility and flagellin protein levels.
source: Furthermore, our data revealed that the C-terminal portion of FliK is critical not only for FliK degradation, but also for its effects on motility and flagellin protein levels.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparison of FliK-C and FliK-CΔ5 effects shown in Figure 5.

claim: Lon has a novel role in coordinating cell differentiation with cell cycle processes in C. crescentus.
source: This study uncovered a novel role of the highly conserved protease Lon in coordinating cell differentiation with cell cycle processes in the dimorphic bacterium C. crescentus.
evidence: This is a conclusion of the study based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Active proteolysis of Lon substrates is required to rapidly clear these proteins following a cell cycle-dependent decrease in their transcription.
source: Our results show that active proteolysis of at least some of these proteins by Lon is required to rapidly clear these proteins following a cell cycle-dependent decrease in their transcription, thus restricting their accumulation to the cell cycle phase when their function is needed (Figure 6).
evidence: This is concluded from the cell cycle synchronization experiments shown in Figures 3 and 5, and summarized in Figure 6.

claim: The abundance of Lon does not change during the cell cycle.
source: The abundance of Lon does not change during the cell cycle (Wright et al., 1996) and a recent study suggested that the catalytic activity of Lon is cell cycle independent (Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from Wright et al., 1996.

claim: The catalytic activity of Lon is cell cycle independent.
source: The abundance of Lon does not change during the cell cycle (Wright et al., 1996) and a recent study suggested that the catalytic activity of Lon is cell cycle independent (Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from Zhou et al., 2019.

claim: Degradation of both SciP and CcrM is modulated by DNA binding.
source: For example, previous work showed that degradation of both SciP and CcrM is modulated by DNA binding (Gora et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2019), and in the case of the AAA+ ATPase DnaA, ATP binding seems to increase protein stability (Liu et al., 2016; Wargachuk and Marczynski, 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Gora et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2019.

claim: ATP binding seems to increase DnaA protein stability.
source: For example, previous work showed that degradation of both SciP and CcrM is modulated by DNA binding (Gora et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2019), and in the case of the AAA+ ATPase DnaA, ATP binding seems to increase protein stability (Liu et al., 2016; Wargachuk and Marczynski, 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Liu et al., 2016; Wargachuk and Marczynski, 2015.

claim: StaR was initially identified as a positive regulator of stalk biogenesis.
source: It was initially identified as a positive regulator of stalk biogenesis (Biondi et al., 2006) and was later shown to regulate holdfast development by directly inhibiting the expression of the holdfast inhibitor HfiA (Fiebig et al., 2014); holdfast is a polysaccharide-rich adhesin that is produced at the nascent stalked cell pole in late swarmer cells and allows C. crescentus to attach to surfaces (Curtis and Brun, 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Biondi et al., 2006.

claim: StaR regulates holdfast development by directly inhibiting the expression of the holdfast inhibitor HfiA.
source: It was initially identified as a positive regulator of stalk biogenesis (Biondi et al., 2006) and was later shown to regulate holdfast development by directly inhibiting the expression of the holdfast inhibitor HfiA (Fiebig et al., 2014); holdfast is a polysaccharide-rich adhesin that is produced at the nascent stalked cell pole in late swarmer cells and allows C. crescentus to attach to surfaces (Curtis and Brun, 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Fiebig et al., 2014.

claim: Holdfast is a polysaccharide-rich adhesin that is produced at the nascent stalked cell pole in late swarmer cells and allows C. crescentus to attach to surfaces.
source: It was initially identified as a positive regulator of stalk biogenesis (Biondi et al., 2006) and was later shown to regulate holdfast development by directly inhibiting the expression of the holdfast inhibitor HfiA (Fiebig et al., 2014); holdfast is a polysaccharide-rich adhesin that is produced at the nascent stalked cell pole in late swarmer cells and allows C. crescentus to attach to surfaces (Curtis and Brun, 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Curtis and Brun, 2010.

claim: Lon may contribute to temporally regulating the abundance of CCNA_02361 during the cell cycle.
source: Thus, Lon may also contribute to temporally regulating the abundance of this protein during the cell cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of CCNA_02361 as a putative Lon substrate and its cell cycle-regulated expression pattern.

claim: FliK proteins function as molecular rulers that precisely measure flagellar hook length via the N-terminal domain and mediate a switch from export of hook protein to filament protein via the C-terminal domain.
source: FliK proteins are thought to function as molecular rulers that, while being exported themselves, precisely measure flagellar hook length via the N-terminal domain and mediate via the C-terminal domain a switch from export of hook protein to filament protein, once the hook has reached a certain length (Erhardt et al., 2011; Minamino, 2018; Minamino et al., 1999; Moriya et al., 2006; Shibata et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from Erhardt et al., 2011; Minamino, 2018; Minamino et al., 1999; Moriya et al., 2006; Shibata et al., 2007.

claim: Proteolytic control mechanisms contributing to FliK regulation have not been described before this study.
source: Although previous work made significant progress in understanding the molecular function of this important protein in enterobacteria, proteolytic control mechanisms contributing to FliK regulation have so far not been described.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that this study addresses.

claim: In bacteria outside the gamma-proteobacteria FliK remains poorly studied.
source: Moreover, in bacteria outside the gamma-proteobacteria FliK remains poorly studied.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: An excess of FliK protein may cause a premature termination of hook synthesis, leading to shorter hooks.
source: Based on studies in other bacteria (Muramoto et al., 1998), we consider it possible that an excess of FliK protein causes a premature termination of hook synthesis, leading to shorter hooks, which may cause downstream effects, namely reduced flagellin levels and motility.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on studies in other bacteria cited from Muramoto et al., 1998.

claim: Overexpressed FliK-C may block the normal function of native FliK by occupying binding sites on interacting proteins.
source: Our observation that overexpression of FliK-C, a truncated version of FliK lacking the N-terminal domain, which is required for export in other bacteria (Hirano et al., 2005), exhibits an even stronger effect on flagellin levels and motility may be explained by a dominant-negative effect that the truncated version of FliK has over the WT. In this scenario, overexpressed FliK-C would block the normal function of native FliK, possibly by occupying binding sites on interacting proteins, for example, the export apparatus protein FlhB (Kinoshita et al., 2017; Minamino et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the stronger effect of FliK-C overexpression, based on citations from Hirano et al., 2005; Kinoshita et al., 2017; Minamino et al., 2009.

claim: The N-terminal domain of FliK is required for export in other bacteria.
source: Our observation that overexpression of FliK-C, a truncated version of FliK lacking the N-terminal domain, which is required for export in other bacteria (Hirano et al., 2005), exhibits an even stronger effect on flagellin levels and motility may be explained by a dominant-negative effect that the truncated version of FliK has over the WT.
evidence: This is cited from Hirano et al., 2005.

claim: The C-terminal five amino acids of FliK are required for its export switch-inducing function in other bacteria.
source: Our result that deletion of the C-terminal five amino acids of Caulobacter FliK-C abolishes the negative overexpression effects (Figure 5F and G) is consistent with the finding that FliK's export switch-inducing function depends on its C-terminal five amino acids in other bacteria (Kinoshita et al., 2017; Minamino et al., 2006; Williams et al., 1996).
evidence: This is cited from Kinoshita et al., 2017; Minamino et al., 2006; Williams et al., 1996.

claim: This study includes a tight coupling between FliK function and degradation.
source: Importantly, we also uncovered a critical role of the C-terminal five amino acids of FliK for proteolytic control (Figure 4G), thus, our data indicate a tight coupling between FliK function and degradation.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that the same C-terminal amino acids are required for both function and degradation.

claim: FlgE was among the proteins that satisfied two criteria in the proteomics approach.
source: Interestingly, in addition to the flagella hook length regulator FliK, our data indicate that the flagella hook protein FlgE itself is regulated by Lon in C. crescentus. FlgE was among the proteins that satisfied two criteria in our proteomics approach, and we verified by Western blot analysis that FlgE degradation partly depends on Lon (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the proteomics analysis.

claim: FlgE degradation partly depends on Lon.
source: Interestingly, in addition to the flagella hook length regulator FliK, our data indicate that the flagella hook protein FlgE itself is regulated by Lon in C. crescentus. FlgE was among the proteins that satisfied two criteria in our proteomics approach, and we verified by Western blot analysis that FlgE degradation partly depends on Lon (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is verified by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lon degrades FlgE in E. coli.
source: This finding is also consistent with previous work showing that Lon degrades FlgE in E. coli (Arends et al., 2018), and reinforces the previously made notion that precise regulation of the cellular concentrations of FlgE as well as FliK is an important requirement for the correct temporal order of flagella assembly (Inoue et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from Arends et al., 2018.

claim: Precise regulation of the cellular concentrations of FlgE as well as FliK is an important requirement for the correct temporal order of flagella assembly.
source: This finding is also consistent with previous work showing that Lon degrades FlgE in E. coli (Arends et al., 2018), and reinforces the previously made notion that precise regulation of the cellular concentrations of FlgE as well as FliK is an important requirement for the correct temporal order of flagella assembly (Inoue et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from Inoue et al., 2018.

claim: Lon has been linked to flagella-mediated motility in several bacteria, including important human pathogens.
source: In several other bacteria, including important human pathogens, Lon has been linked to flagella-mediated motility (Ching et al., 2019; Clemmer and Rather, 2008; Fuchs et al., 2001; Rogers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Ching et al., 2019; Clemmer and Rather, 2008; Fuchs et al., 2001; Rogers et al., 2016.

claim: In Bacillus subtilis, Lon specifically degrades the master regulator of flagellar biosynthesis SwrA by a mechanism requiring the adaptor SmiA.
source: However, in Bacillus subtilis, it was shown that Lon specifically degrades the master regulator of flagellar biosynthesis SwrA by a mechanism requiring the adaptor SmiA (Mukherjee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Mukherjee et al., 2015.

claim: Both StaR and FliK are robustly degraded by Lon in vitro.
source: In contrast to SwrA, both StaR and FliK are robustly degraded by Lon in vitro (Figures 2D and 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on in vitro degradation assay data shown in Figures 2D, 4F, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: No adaptors or other accessory proteins are required to mediate the interaction between StaR/FliK and Lon in vitro.
source: While these data suggest that no adaptors or other accessory proteins are required to mediate the interaction between these proteins and Lon, it is possible that additional factors exist that modulate the rate of Lon-mediated proteolysis of these proteins in response to specific conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vitro degradation assays, but with the caveat that additional factors may exist in vivo.
